digest.top_line: AGITG MASTERPLAN: adding SBRT 40 Gy/5fx to chemo cut 12-mo LRR 20.2% vs 52.0% (P=0.022), mOS 22.0 vs 14.0 mo in high-risk operable/borderline/LA pancreas.
digest.tldr: Local control led the day. MASTERPLAN isolates the SBRT benefit on LRR in pancreas. UNION's 3-yr EFS 91.3% vs 77.4% (HR 0.33) in LARC bundles SCRT with camrelizumab, so the RT share can't be separated. TOP-1 points the other way: omitting RT and ET at age ≥70 gave 5-yr LR 14.8%, with the lower CI bound above the 10% threshold.

sites.intro: I-124 PET-selected RAI de-escalation in DTC halves blood dose, but the primary endpoint is a surrogate and EFS has few events.

studies.name: CLERAD-PROBE
studies.tldr: Mean blood dose 275 vs 521 mGy (p<0.001) with I-124 PET-guided risk-adapted vs broad adjuvant RAI in DTC; 5y EFS 96.6% vs 91.5%.
details: 🔍 Prospective randomized bicentric trial, N=324 enrolled May 2015 to May 2021 (155 Arm 1, 169 Arm 2)
🔍 Adult DTC post-thyroidectomy; unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm excluded

details.text: 🔍 Arm 1 RIT triggers (after I-124 PET staging)
subdetails: Distant metastases or iodine-avid lesions on PET

details: 🔍 Arm 2: RIT generally performed

details.text: 📊 Outcomes, risk-adapted vs broad RIT (median f/u 64 mo)

details: 📊 I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 (14.1%) postop T1/T2 N0/Nx pts to N1, triggering RIT
⚠️ Primary endpoint is blood dose, a surrogate for secondary malignancy risk, not oncologic outcome
⚠️ EFS is secondary with few events; not a powered non-inferiority comparison
⚠️ Sex imbalance: fewer males in Arm 1 (19% vs 34%, p=0.002)
⚠️ Arm 1 bundles PET staging with selective omission; can't separate PET's upstaging from de-escalation itself
🔗 Sits alongside ESTIMABL2 and IoN, which tested RAI omission in low-risk DTC; here selection is imaging-driven rather than pathology alone

verdict.rationale: Randomized, primary met, but primary is a dosimetric surrogate; the oncologic-safety claim rests on a secondary EFS with 19 events, unpowered for non-inferiority, plus sex imbalance.
verdict.audience: Adult DTC post-thyroidectomy, excluding unifocal PTMC ≤10 mm

studies.significance: The decision-carrying detail is PET's upstaging: 11 of 78 (14.1%) pts with postop T1/T2 N0/Nx were N1 on I-124 PET and got RIT, so the de-escalation arm still treated occult nodal disease. Activity roughly halved (2.5 vs 5.7 GBq) with no EFS signal against it, informing omission in imaging-negative, low-risk DTC.
studies.monday_clinic: In adult DTC after thyroidectomy with no risk factors on I-124 PET staging, this supports omitting adjuvant RAI; it does not extend to selection without PET or to pts with incomplete resection, extrathyroidal extent or distant disease.

primary_endpoint.name: Mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective, **randomized, bicentric** trial (NCT01704586); 324 pts enrolled May 2015 to May 2021. **Median follow-up 64 months**, maximum planned 10 years.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adult DTC after thyroidectomy. **Unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm excluded.** Arms matched for histology, age and stage, but Arm 1 had fewer males (19% vs 34%, p=0.002).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Arm 1: I-124 PET staging, then RIT **only with risk factors** (incomplete resection, tumor >4 cm, extrathyroidal extent, LN metastases with age ≥45 years, distant metastases, or iodine-avid lesions on PET). Arm 2: RIT generally given. Administered activity **2.5 vs 5.7 GBq**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months, a surrogate for secondary malignancy risk. **Secondary:** event-free survival.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: PET upstaged **11 of 78 (14.1%)** postop T1/T2 N0/Nx pts to N1. Recurrence and EFS numerically favored the risk-adapted arm, with borderline p-values (0.06 and 0.05).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ESTIMABL2 and IoN addressed RAI omission in low-risk DTC selected on pathology; CLERAD-PROBE adds functional I-124 PET to the selection step and spans a broader risk range. Guidelines still diverge on adjuvant RAI, which is the gap this trial targets.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adult DTC post-thyroidectomy staged with I-124 PET, where RIT is reserved for defined risk factors. Does not represent unifocal papillary microcarcinoma ≤10 mm or centers without I-124 PET.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: PET staging and selective omission are bundled in one arm, so the dose saving cannot be credited to omission alone. The sex imbalance favors Arm 1 prognostically, and the abstract gives no toxicity or secondary-malignancy data.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Blood dose roughly halved with no signal of worse recurrence, supporting de-escalation in selected pts. Whether **lower exposure translates into fewer second cancers** remains unmeasured, and the event count can't exclude a modest EFS deficit.

studies.interpretation:
The adjuvant radioiodine question in differentiated thyroid cancer has never had a clean answer, partly because the benefit being protected is small and the harm being avoided, second malignancy, is rare and late. CLERAD-PROBE takes the harm side seriously by making blood dose its primary endpoint. The trial wins clearly on that endpoint, but blood dose is a dosimetric surrogate. It tells you exposure fell, not that cancers were prevented. A reader should treat the primary result as near-certain and its clinical meaning as inferred.

The more interesting design choice is that the risk-adapted arm is not simply RAI omission. Every pt in Arm 1 went through I-124 PET first, and PET moved 11 of 78 (14.1%) pathologically low-stage pts into the nodal-positive group that received treatment. That differs from ESTIMABL2 and IoN, which selected low-risk pts on surgical pathology and asked whether ablation could be dropped. Here the comparison is a functional-imaging-guided strategy versus near-universal treatment. A center that adopts selective omission without PET is not running the CLERAD-PROBE strategy, and the trial cannot say how much of the oncologic result depends on catching occult nodes.

The oncologic data need careful handling. Recurrence and EFS point toward the risk-adapted arm (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.14-1.05, p=0.06; 5y EFS 96.6% vs 91.5%), which is the opposite of what one fears from de-escalation. But 19 total events cannot carry a non-inferiority claim, and a numerically better outcome in the less-treated arm should make a reader look for imbalance before crediting the strategy. One is reported: Arm 1 enrolled fewer men (19% vs 34%). Male sex is generally an adverse factor in DTC, so that imbalance plausibly tilts EFS toward Arm 1. PET-driven treatment of occult nodes is another candidate explanation. The defensible reading is that the trial shows no sign of harm, not that de-escalation improves control.

For practice, the result supports selective RAI when staging is thorough, and it frames I-124 PET as part of the selection rather than an optional extra. It does not settle whether the second-malignancy reduction is real at the scale that would justify the imaging cost. It also leaves open whether intermediate-risk pts with only one marginal factor fare as well. The full paper will need toxicity, salivary and late outcomes, and the planned 10-year EFS. The abstract reports none of these, and they would decide whether the dose saving is worth anything clinically.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 (14.1%) apparently N0/Nx pts to N1, so the de-escalation arm still treated occult nodal disease. Activity fell from 5.7 to 2.5 GBq with no EFS signal against it, informing radioiodine omission in imaging-negative, low-risk DTC.

open_questions: Does lower blood dose reduce second malignancies long term?
Is risk-adapted omission safe without I-124 PET staging?
Does EFS hold at the planned 10-year follow-up?

sites.intro: SCRT-based TNT plus PD-1 blockade beats LCCRT on EFS, but the pCR primary endpoint is not reported in source.

studies.name: UNION
studies.tldr: 3-yr EFS 91.3% vs 77.4%, HR 0.33 (0.15-0.71), P=0.0029: SCRT → camrelizumab + CAPOX vs long-course CRT → CAPOX in LARC.
details: ⚠️ Primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pCR rate; the pCR result is not reported in the source abstract
📊 EFS is a key secondary endpoint with prespecified α allocation; BIRC-assessed EFS also favored the experimental arm
🔍 Phase 3, 1:1, N=231 randomized (113 vs 118), July 2021 to March 2023

subdetails: Exp: SCRT 25 Gy/5f → 2 neoadjuvant + 6 adjuvant CAPOX, camrelizumab 200 mg d1 for up to 17 cycles
SOC: 50.4 Gy/28f with capecitabine 825 mg/m2 BID → same 2 + 6 CAPOX
Surgery type and timing not reported in source

details: ⚠️ Two variables change at once (RT schedule and PD-1 inhibitor), so neither SCRT nor IO effect can be isolated
⚠️ Safety denominators (115 vs 112) differ from randomized counts (113 vs 118), so the as-treated populations differ from ITT
⚠️ OS not reported in source; MMR/MSI breakdown of the enrolled cohort not reported
🔗 SCRT-based TNT precedent: RAPIDO; LCCRT-based TNT: PRODIGE 23. UNION adds a PD-1 inhibitor to an SCRT backbone

verdict.rationale: Randomized phase 3, but the primary pCR result is not in source and EFS is secondary. SCRT and camrelizumab change together, so the benefit cannot be attributed to either.
verdict.audience: cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma ≤10 cm from anal verge

studies.significance: The control is long-course CRT, so the EFS gain (HR 0.33) comes with a switch to 25 Gy/5f. That makes SCRT the RT backbone for an IO-containing TNT, not a compromise. Because RT schedule and camrelizumab were changed together, the trial cannot say whether SCRT itself is what lets IO work in largely pMMR disease.
studies.monday_clinic: In cT3-4 or node-positive low/mid rectal adenocarcinoma, this supports SCRT followed by PD-1 inhibitor plus CAPOX as an evidence-backed TNT option. It does not settle IO use when no PD-1 agent equivalent to camrelizumab is available, or questions of organ preservation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3**, randomized 1:1, **N=231** (113 vs 118), accrued July 2021 to March 2023. Median follow-up 36.8 vs 35.6 mo at the October 1, 2025 cutoff.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **cT3-4 or N+** rectal adenocarcinoma, tumor **≤10 cm from the anal verge**. MMR/MSI composition of the enrolled cohort is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Experimental: **SCRT 25 Gy/5f**. Control: **50.4 Gy/28f** with concurrent capecitabine 825 mg/m2 BID. Target volumes are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: 2 neoadjuvant + 6 adjuvant cycles of CAPOX. Experimental adds **camrelizumab 200 mg d1** given alongside CAPOX for up to 17 cycles.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** BIRC-assessed pCR rate (result not in source). Key secondary endpoints with prespecified α: investigator-assessed EFS and OS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G≥3 TRAE over the whole treatment period **51.3% (59/115) vs 48.2% (54/112)**. The RT-attributable split is not reported.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RAPIDO set SCRT followed by consolidation chemo as a TNT option, and PRODIGE 23 did the same for an LCCRT-based approach. UNION is the first phase 3 to layer a PD-1 inhibitor onto SCRT in LARC, building on earlier SCRT + IO phase 2 signals such as TORCH.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma ≤10 cm from the anal verge treated with curative-intent TNT. Does not represent upper rectal tumors beyond 10 cm, watch-and-wait candidates, or settings without camrelizumab.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The safety population (115 vs 112) does not match randomization (113 vs 118), so some pts received the other arm's treatment. Neoadjuvant CAPOX was only 2 cycles in the control arm, lighter than full TNT backbones. OS and surgical or organ-preservation outcomes are absent.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The EFS effect is large and was tested under alpha control, but it comes from a **two-variable comparison**. It supports the whole package and does not establish what SCRT or camrelizumab contributes individually.

studies.interpretation:
UNION is a package trial. The experimental arm differs from control in two ways at once: the radiation schedule moves from 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions with capecitabine to 25 Gy in 5, and a PD-1 inhibitor is added through the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases. An EFS hazard ratio of 0.33 therefore tells the reader that the combined strategy beats long-course chemoradiation followed by CAPOX. It does not tell them whether short-course RT is the better partner for immunotherapy, whether camrelizumab would deliver the same gain after long-course CRT, or whether the schedule change is neutral and IO does all the work. The biological rationale for pairing hypofractionated RT with PD-1 blockade (immunogenic cell death, less lymphodepletion from a short course) is exactly what this design cannot test. A factorial or a third arm would have been needed.

The second issue is hierarchy. The registered primary endpoint was BIRC-assessed pCR, and the presented abstract does not give that result. EFS is a key secondary with its own alpha allocation, so the P=0.0029 is not a post-hoc finding. Still, a reader is entitled to see the primary before accepting the authors' new-standard claim, especially since pCR is the endpoint most directly tied to the immunotherapy hypothesis.

The magnitude is also striking for a trial of 231 pts. The confidence interval on the HR (0.15-0.71) is wide, and the 3-yr EFS estimates have overlapping intervals at their edges. A control arm at 77.4% is within the plausible range for this population, but the experimental arm's 91.3% sits high enough that replication in a non-Chinese population, with a PD-1 agent available elsewhere, matters before generalizing. The MMR/MSI composition of the cohort is not given. If any dMMR pts were included and were unevenly distributed, they could carry a disproportionate share of the IO effect.

Against RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23, UNION is better read as an IO extension of the SCRT-based TNT lineage than as a replacement of it: the control arm's neoadjuvant chemotherapy was only two CAPOX cycles, lighter than the consolidation those trials established. A modern full-TNT comparator might narrow the gap. Toxicity looks acceptable on the reported G≥3 TRAE rates, but the mismatch between randomized and safety denominators suggests crossover or as-treated reassignment, which should be clarified in the full report. Organ preservation, surgical morbidity and OS will decide whether this becomes practice. For a radiation oncologist, the actionable point today is that 25 Gy/5f held up as the RT component of an intensified, IO-containing curative regimen.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The experimental arm swapped 50.4 Gy/28f chemoRT for 25 Gy/5f and still improved 3-yr EFS (91.3% vs 77.4%). That puts SCRT forward as the RT platform for IO consolidation. Whether SCRT is synergistic or just interchangeable cannot be separated from the camrelizumab effect.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Adding camrelizumab across neoadjuvant and adjuvant CAPOX (up to 17 cycles) gave EFS HR 0.33 with G≥3 TRAE 51.3% vs 48.2%. It is a signal for PD-1 blockade beyond dMMR in LARC, though the MMR breakdown and OS are not in source, and camrelizumab availability outside China limits how far it transfers.

open_questions: Does SCRT, versus long-course CRT, drive the immunotherapy benefit?
Unreported pCR primary result and OS
Benefit in confirmed pMMR/MSS pts specifically

sites.intro: TOP-1 tests omitting both RT and ET in low-risk elderly ER+ BC; 5-yr LR exceeds the bound the design was meant to exclude.

studies.name: TOP-1 (BOOG 2016-01)
studies.tldr: 5-yr local recurrence 14.8% (95% CI 12.3-17.5) after BCS alone without RT or ET in women ≥70 with low-risk ER+ HER2- BC.
details: 📊 5-yr LR 14.8% (95% CI 12.3-17.5): 123 invasive ipsilateral events in 792 pts
⚠️ Lower CI bound 12.3% exceeds the 10% 5-yr LR the study was powered to exclude
🔍 Prospective, multicenter, observational, single-arm; N=792 (800 planned), accrual Jan 2017 to Sep 2021
🔍 Women ≥70, ER ≥50%, HER2-negative, ≤1cm grade 1/2 or ≤2cm grade 1, free margins
💊 No ET by design: Dutch guidelines do not advise ET in T1 low-grade early-stage BC
🔍 Median age 73.6y, median f/u 5.1y (IQR 4.9-5.2); cumulative incidence with death as competing event
🔗 Design assumption: 1.3% (99% CI 0.6-2.5%) 5-yr LR with RT from national registry; upper limit tripled to 7.5% without RT
⚠️ Comparator is a historical registry, not a concurrent RT arm; RT-attributable effect not directly estimable
⚠️ RT and ET both omitted: cannot apportion the excess LR between the two

verdict.rationale: Single-arm observational cohort against a historical registry benchmark; no concurrent RT or ET arm, and 5.1y f/u is short for low-grade ER+ recurrence kinetics.
verdict.audience: Women ≥70, low-risk ER+ HER2- T1 BC after BCS, no endocrine therapy

studies.significance: The trial removed endocrine therapy as well as RT, which earlier omission trials never did, and LR reached 14.8%, above the 10% ceiling it was powered to exclude. Salvage was mostly feasible (86 repeat BCS), but 70 pts received RT at recurrence anyway. So in ET-untreated older women, omitting RT often postpones it rather than avoiding it.
studies.monday_clinic: In a woman ≥70 with ≤2cm low-grade ER+ HER2- BC after BCS who will not take ET, this questions RT omission as low-risk; it does not test RT omission in women who do take ET.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective, multicenter, observational, **single-arm** cohort; **N=792** of 800 planned (80% power to exclude a **10% 5-yr LR**). Median f/u **5.1y**; cumulative incidence with death as competing event.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Women **≥70y**, **ER ≥50%, HER2-negative**, ≤1cm grade 1/2 or ≤2cm grade 1, **free margins**, after BCS with **no RT and no ET**. Median age 73.6y.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** 5-yr LR, a histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral event. Secondary: contralateral BC, OS, BC-specific survival.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **5-yr LR 14.8% (95% CI 12.3-17.5)**, exceeding the prespecified 10% threshold. 2 of 81 deaths BC-related.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PRIME II and CALGB 9343 supported RT omission in older women who **received ET**; TOP-1 tests the population that skips both. The trial's own benchmark is a national registry LR of **1.3%** with RT, not a randomized arm.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women ≥70 with low-risk ER+ HER2- T1 BC after BCS who receive neither RT nor ET. Does not represent older women who take adjuvant ET after RT omission.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Only invasive ipsilateral events counted, so DCIS recurrence is excluded from the primary. Registry comparator differs in era and selection, and ER+ low-grade recurrences accrue well beyond 5y.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Dropping both adjuvant therapies **failed the study's own safety bar**, while salvage remained mostly breast-conserving. The authors keep RT omission as a shared-decision option, but the result does not show which omitted therapy drove the excess.

studies.interpretation:
The RT omission evidence that shapes current practice in older women with small ER+ tumors comes from trials in which every patient took endocrine therapy. PRIME II and CALGB 9343 showed that whole-breast RT could be dropped with acceptable local control, but the low recurrence attributed to omitting RT was always partly an ET effect. TOP-1 removes that support. It studies the group Dutch guidelines already leave without ET and asks whether breast-conserving surgery alone is enough. At a median 5.1 years the answer falls short of the investigators' own bar. Local recurrence was 14.8%, and the lower confidence bound of 12.3% sits above the 10% ceiling the study was powered to exclude, a ceiling patient advocates had accepted in advance. This is a prespecified threshold failure, not a judgement made after the fact.

Several design features should raise confidence in the direction of the result. Accrual reached 792 of 800 planned across multiple centers. The analysis used cumulative incidence with death as a competing event, which is the right method in a cohort where 81 patients died; a naive Kaplan-Meier estimate would have overstated recurrence. The primary endpoint counted only histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral events, so DCIS recurrences are excluded, and the full ipsilateral event burden is if anything higher than 14.8%. What limits the reading is the comparator. The 1.3% figure with RT comes from a national registry, not a concurrent arm, so the RT-attributable reduction cannot be estimated from this study. Selection and era differences between registry and cohort cannot account for a gap this wide unless the registry population was very different, and nothing in the source suggests that.

The central point the trial cannot settle is apportionment. RT and ET were both omitted, so the excess recurrence reflects the loss of both, and a reader cannot tell how much returns if only one is given. EUROPA, which compares RT alone with ET alone in older women, addresses that choice directly. TOP-1 therefore argues against omitting both adjuvant therapies in this population. It says nothing against the established practice of omitting RT in women who take ET.

The authors' case for keeping omission available rests on salvage and survival. Of 123 recurrences, 114 were treated surgically and 86 had repeat BCS, and only 2 of 81 deaths were breast cancer related. That survival signal is reassuring but early: low-grade ER+ disease relapses slowly, and five years is too short to show whether recurrence affects breast cancer mortality. The salvage numbers also show a cost the headline hides. 70 patients received RT at recurrence, so for a large share of those who relapsed, omission postponed radiotherapy, added a second operation, and moved both to an older age. A shared decision about omission without ET should present it as accepting roughly one-in-seven local recurrence by five years, with RT and surgery still likely if that happens, rather than avoiding treatment.

The conclusion would be wrong if longer follow-up showed that recurrences plateau after five years while competing mortality rises, which would shrink the absolute lifetime cost. That seems unlikely for ER+ disease, whose recurrence hazard tends to persist late.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: In women ≥70 with low-risk ER+ disease, omitting RT without ET gave 14.8% 5-yr LR, and 70 of 123 recurrences received RT at salvage. Without ET, RT omission often means postponed RT, which reframes the omission conversation for pts declining or not offered ET.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Dutch guidelines do not advise ET for T1 low-grade ER+ BC, and this cohort shows what happens when RT is also dropped: 14.8% 5-yr LR. For pts in whom RT is omitted, the decision to withhold ET as well now carries a measured local cost.

open_questions: LR with ET alone after RT omission in this exact population
Breast cancer-specific survival impact beyond 5 years
Genomic or biomarker selection for safe omission of both RT and ET

🔍 SBRT 40 Gy in 5 fx, fiducial guidance, real-time RT QA
⚠️ Only 39 of 49 (80%) assigned to SBRT actually started it; ITT read dilutes RT effect
⚠️ Small N with mixed operable/inoperable pts; OS and PFS are secondary endpoints
⚠️ IPC stratum (n=26) underpowered; LRR difference there not significant
⚠️ G3+ toxicity high in both arms; RT-attributable late GI toxicity not reported in source

verdict.rationale: Randomized with primary endpoint met, but N=74 across heterogeneous strata, 80% SBRT uptake, and OS/PFS secondary; phase not stated, conference trade-press source only.
verdict.audience: High-risk operable, borderline resectable, or locally advanced pancreatic cancer

studies.significance: The LRR benefit held in the potentially operable stratum (19.7% vs 52.9%, P=0.031) but not the inoperable one (P=0.16, n=26), so the strongest RT read is neoadjuvant SBRT 40 Gy/5fx after 3 mo of modern chemo in borderline or high-risk operable disease. That benefit came despite only 80% of the SBRT arm starting RT.
studies.monday_clinic: In borderline resectable or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer after 3 mo of mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel, this supports considering SBRT 40 Gy/5fx before surgical reassessment; the inoperable-stratum signal is too small to settle locally advanced disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized 2:1**, chemo + SBRT vs chemo alone, 75 enrolled and **74 eligible** across 14 centers. Phase not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Potentially operable (n=48):** borderline resectable, or operable with tumor >4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, or nodal involvement. **Inoperable (n=26):** locally advanced or medically inoperable.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Three months of **mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel** by clinician choice, then reassessment for surgery. Resected pts received 3 more months adjuvant; unresected pts 3 more months systemic chemo.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT 40 Gy in 5 fractions** with fiducial marker guidance and real-time RT quality assurance. **39 of 49 (80%)** assigned to SBRT initiated it.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: locoregional recurrence at 12 months.** Secondary: PFS, OS, surgical outcomes, toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint met; benefit significant in the potentially operable stratum, **not significant in inoperable disease (P=0.16)**. Resection and R0 rates numerically higher with SBRT, both non-significant.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: G3+ toxicity **70.2% vs 64.0% (P=0.27)**, no significant increase with SBRT. RT-specific and late toxicity not broken out in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Randomized evidence for adding RT to chemo in pancreatic cancer has been inconsistent: LAP07 tested conventional chemoRT in locally advanced disease, and PREOPANC tested preoperative chemoRT in resectable and borderline disease. MASTERPLAN differs by pairing short-course SBRT with modern multiagent chemo and by powering on local control rather than OS.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents borderline resectable or high-risk operable pancreatic cancer receiving 3 mo of mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel before SBRT 40 Gy/5fx. Does not represent standard-risk resectable disease, and the locally advanced/inoperable stratum is too small to support a conclusion.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Incomplete SBRT uptake (80%) and clinician-chosen chemo add noise to a small trial. The OS gain sits on a secondary endpoint with no HR reported in the source, and late GI toxicity is not described.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A local control benefit of this size, carried into PFS and OS, makes a larger confirmatory trial a priority. It does not yet settle which stratum benefits, whether the OS signal is real, or how SBRT should be sequenced with surgery.

studies.interpretation:
The question MASTERPLAN asks is an old one in pancreatic cancer: once systemic therapy controls micrometastatic disease better, does local failure become a problem worth radiating? Earlier randomized work mostly said no, or said it unclearly. LAP07 tested conventionally fractionated chemoradiation in locally advanced disease against a chemotherapy backbone that is now outdated, and PREOPANC tested preoperative chemoradiation in resectable and borderline disease. Neither used ablative-range stereotactic dosing, and neither was designed around local control as the primary question. MASTERPLAN changes both variables at once. It uses 40 Gy in five fractions with fiducials and real-time QA, and it puts locoregional recurrence at 12 months first, which is the endpoint SBRT can most directly move.

On that endpoint the result is clear, and the absolute gap is large enough that a trial of 74 patients could detect it. The difference in median OS from 14.0 to 22.0 months (P=0.006) is what will get attention, and also where caution is most needed. OS was secondary, the source reports no hazard ratio or confidence interval, and the trial was not powered for survival. Small randomized trials in pancreatic cancer have produced survival differences before that did not hold up at scale. The direction is coherent, because better local control, longer PFS (11.9 vs 6.3 months) and longer OS all point the same way. Still, coherence is not confirmation, and the reported OS gain is larger than one would expect from a local therapy alone when distant failure remains the dominant pattern.

Two design features should shape how far a reader generalizes. First, the population is mixed. The benefit is driven by the potentially operable stratum, while the inoperable stratum (n=26) shows a similar point estimate but does not reach significance. A radiation oncologist treating locally advanced disease should not take the pooled result as settling that setting. Second, only 80% of patients assigned to SBRT started it. That would normally bias an intention-to-treat comparison toward the null, so the true per-protocol effect on local control may be larger. It also means a fifth of the experimental arm did not get the intervention, and the source does not say why. If early progression or deconditioning was the reason, the issue is selection for SBRT fitness, not dilution.

The surgical data are honest non-results. Resection (68% vs 59%) and R0 rates (62% vs 40%) favor SBRT numerically but are underpowered. A surgeon should not read them as evidence that SBRT converts resectability. Toxicity is reassuring at the G3+ aggregate level, but that figure is dominated by chemotherapy, and the late duodenal and gastric effects that matter for stereotactic pancreatic RT are not described.

For the result to be wrong, the control arm's locoregional recurrence would need to be unusually high by chance, or recurrence assessment would need to be biased in an unblinded trial. The next trial should be larger, restricted by stratum, report RT-specific late toxicity, and test whether the OS signal survives.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: SBRT 40 Gy/5fx after 3 mo of modern chemo cut 12-mo LRR to 19.7% vs 52.9% in potentially operable disease (P=0.031), despite 80% SBRT uptake. The inoperable stratum (P=0.16, n=26) leaves locally advanced SBRT unsettled.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Neoadjuvant SBRT gave numerically higher resection (68% vs 59%, P=0.54) and R0 (62% vs 40%, P=0.44) in potentially operable pts. Neither difference is significant, so this does not yet show SBRT improves resectability, but it shows no surgical penalty.

Does SBRT benefit locally advanced/inoperable disease specifically?

papers.title: Omission of adjuvant radiotherapy after breast-conserving surgery in systemically untreated older patients with early-stage estrogen receptor positive breast cancer: 5-year results of the TOP-1 study (BOOG 2016-01)
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 545RO · Rapid oral: Breast cancer, early stage · 2026-10-23 · presented by Lotte Bouwman (Leiden, Netherlands)

Background: Adjuvant radiotherapy (RT) following breast-conserving surgery (BCS) is standard of care in women with early-stage estrogen-receptor positive (ER+) breast cancer (BC). Previous studies on RT omission involved older patients treated with BCS and endocrine therapy (ET), showing low local recurrence (LR) risks. According to Dutch guidelines, ET is not advised in T1, low-grade early-stage BC. This study assessed 5-year LR risk after BCS without RT, in older patients with ER+ BC without ET.
Methods: The prospective, multicenter, observational, single-arm TOP-1 study included women aged ≥70 years with low-risk BC (ER+ ≥50%, HER2-negative, ≤1cm and grade 1/2, or ≤2cm grade 1 with free surgical margins). Primary endpoint was 5-year LR risk, defined as a histologically confirmed invasive ipsilateral event. Secondary endpoints included contralateral BC, overall and BC specific survival. Cumulative incidence analysis was performed with death as competing event. With a 1.3% (99%CI 0.6-2.5%; national registry) 5-year LR risk with RT, and the upper CI limit tripled without RT (7.5%), 800 patients (power 80%) were needed to exclude a 10% 5-year LR risk, acceptable to patient advocates.
Results: Between January 2017 and September 2021, 792 patients were included. Median age was 73.6 years (IQI 71.9-75.5). Median follow-up was 5.1 years (IQR 4.9-5.2). In total, 123 patients developed a LR, resulting in a 5-year LR risk of 14.8% (95%CI 12.3-17.5). Treatment of LR was surgical in 114 (92.7%) patients, of whom 86 (75.4%) BCS, 70 (56.7%) patients received RT and 43 (35.0%) ET. Contralateral BC was diagnosed in 32 (4.0%) patients. Death occurred in 81 (10.2%) patients, of whom 2 (2.5%) BC related.
Conclusions: Omission of adjuvant RT resulted in a 5-year LR risk of 14.8% after BCS without ET, in women aged ≥70 with low-grade T1, ER+ BC. Although the LR risk exceeded prior estimates, BCS was possible in most patients and BC specific survival was excellent. Therefore, in a shared decision setting, RT omission is an option for a subgroup of older patients. Follow-up is needed to assess longer-term survival and other secondary endpoints.
Clinical trial identification: National Trial Register: 6147 (however, nowadays outdated). Also registered in the CCMO Research Portal as NL-008797.

papers.title: I-124 PET-guided risk-adapted versus broad adjuvant radioiodine therapy in differentiated thyroid carcinoma: Results from the randomized CLERAD-PROBE trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 4210RO · Rapid oral: NETs and endocrine tumours · 2026-10-23 · presented by Kerstin Michalski (Wuerzburg, Germany) · NCT01704586

Background: The role of adjuvant radioiodine therapy (RIT) in differentiated thyroid carcinoma (DTC) remains controversial due to diverging international guidelines. The CLERAD-PROBE trial compares a risk-adapted with a broad RIT strategy regarding blood dose — as surrogate for secondary malignancy risk — and oncological outcomes.
Methods: CLERAD-PROBE is a prospective, randomized, bicentric study (NCT01704586) in adult DTC patients, excluding unifocal papillary microcarcinomas ≤10 mm. Following thyroidectomy, patients in Arm 1 underwent I-124 PET for staging; RIT was administered only if risk factors were present (incomplete resection, tumor >4 cm, extrathyroidal extent, lymph node metastases with age ≥45 years, distant metastases, or iodine-avid lesions on PET). In Arm 2, RIT was generally performed. The primary endpoint was mean blood dose at complete remission or 18 months; the secondary endpoint was event-free survival with a maximum follow-up of 10 years.
Results: 324 patients were enrolled from May 2015 to May 2021 (155 Arm 1, 169 Arm 2). Arms were well-matched for histology, age, and tumor stage; however, Arm 1 included fewer male patients (19% vs. 34%, p=0.002). Notably, I-124 PET upstaged 11 of 78 patients (14.1%) with postoperative T1/T2 and N0/Nx to N1, prompting RIT in these cases. Mean blood dose (275 vs. 521 mGy; p<0.001) and administered activity (2.5 vs. 5.7 GBq; p<0.001) were significantly lower in Arm 1. Median follow-up was 64 months. In Arm 1, risk of progressive or recurrent disease was lower (5 cases in Arm 1 vs. 14 in Arm 2; hazard ratio: 0.38; 95% CI: 0.14-1.05; p=0.06) and event-free survival higher (Log-rank test: p=0.05). Five-year event-free survival was 96.6% in Arm 1 vs. 91.5% in Arm 2.
Conclusions: CLERAD-PROBE demonstrates that a risk-adapted, PET-guided RIT strategy significantly reduces radiation exposure without evidence of inferior oncological outcomes. While the low number of events warrants cautious interpretation, the results support the oncological safety of RIT de-escalation and provide a rationale for a risk-adapted approach in appropriately selected DTC patients.
Clinical trial identification: NCT01704586.

papers.title: Neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy followed by camrelizumab and chemotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC): The phase 3 UNION trial
papers.abstract:
ESMO Congress 2026 abstract 3530O · Proffered paper: Gastrointestinal tumours, lower digestive · 2026-10-25 · presented by Zhen Yu Lin (Wuhan, China) · NCT04928807

Background: Despite the use of neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, recurrence and distant metastasis remain common in LARC. Effective immunotherapy-based strategies for the predominantly proficient mismatch repair/microsatellite-stable population remain limited. UNION is the first phase 3 trial to evaluate a neoadjuvant strategy incorporating radiotherapy, immunotherapy, and chemotherapy in LARC. Here we present the prespecified event-free survival (EFS) analysis.
Methods: Patients with cT3-4 or N+ rectal adenocarcinoma (tumor located ≤10 cm from the anal verge) were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive short-course radiotherapy (SCRT; 25 Gy/5f; experimental group) or long-course chemoradiotherapy (50.4 Gy/28f with concurrent capecitabine 825 mg/m2 twice daily; standard of care group) followed by 2 neoadjuvant cycles and 6 adjuvant cycles of capecitabine and oxaliplatin (CAPOX). The experimental group additionally received neoadjuvant and adjuvant camrelizumab (200 mg, day 1) since CAPOX treatment for up to 17 cycles. The primary endpoint was blinded independent review committee (BIRC)-assessed pathological complete response rate. Key secondary endpoints with prespecified α allocation were investigator-assessed EFS and overall survival.
Results: Between July 2021 and March 2023, 231 patients were randomized to the experimental group (n=113) and standard of care group (n=118). As of October 1, 2025, the median follow-up duration was 36.8 months (95% CI, 34.8-37.8) and 35.6 months (95% CI, 34.3-36.9), respectively. The 3-year EFS rate was significantly higher in the experimental group compared with standard of care (91.3% [95% CI, 83.9-95.4] vs 77.4% [95% CI, 67.9-84.4], hazard ratio=0.33 [95% CI, 0.15-0.71], P=0.0029). BIRC-assessed EFS consistently favored the experimental group. During the whole treatment period, the incidence of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events was 51.3% (59/115) and 48.2% (54/112), respectively.
Conclusions: UNION is the first phase 3 trial to demonstrate a significant improvement in EFS with an immunotherapy-based regimen in LARC. This neoadjuvant strategy represents a new standard of care.
Clinical trial identification: NCT04928807.
